people.Kilix: Brother of Kadmos, who gave up the search and settled Kilikia. Apollod. 3.1.1
people.Phoinix: Brother of Kadmos, who gave his name to Phoenicia. Apollod. 3.1.1

Kyparissos.note: Loved by Apollo. He killed a tame stag by accident and grieved so long that he asked to mourn for ever, and was turned into the CYPRESS, the tree that stands in graveyards still. Ov. Met. 10.106-142

Krokos.note: Loved by Hermes, who killed him by accident with a discus in the same way; from his blood came the CROCUS, and from the crocus, saffron. Ov. Fasti 5.227

Ampelos.note: A satyr youth loved by Dionysos, killed by a wild bull, and turned into the first grapevine -- ampelos, whence ampelography, the study of vines. Nonnus, Dionysiaca 10-12

Daphnis.note: A Sicilian herdsman, son of Hermes, loved by Pan and by a nymph; he invented pastoral poetry and died of love. Theokritos 1

people.Hylas: Herakles' armour-bearer and beloved, taken by the water-nymphs of a spring in Mysia when he stooped to fill his jar. Herakles searched the whole coast shouting his name and the Argo sailed without him. Apollod. 1.9.19, Theokritos 13

Koronis.note: Loved by Apollo and unfaithful while carrying his child; a white crow brought the news and Apollo, in anger, scorched it black -- which is why crows are black -- and killed her, snatching the baby from the pyre. Apollod. 3.10.3, Ov. Met. 2.542-632

Kyrene.note: A huntress who wrestled a lion bare-handed; Apollo watched, asked Cheiron who she was, and carried her to Libya, where the city of Cyrene is named for her. Pind. Pyth. 9

Aristaios.note: Son of Apollo and Kyrene, who taught men beekeeping, cheese and the olive -- the gentlest of the demigods, and the one Vergil's fourth Georgic is about. Aristaios pursued Eurydike, and she trod on the snake fleeing him. Ap. Rhod. 4.1132, Georg. 4.315-558

Chione.note: Loved by Hermes and Apollo on the same night, and bore a son to each: Autolykos the thief and Philammon the singer. Ov. Met. 11.301-317

Autolykos.note: The most accomplished thief alive, who could change the look of anything he stole -- his father's gift. Grandfather of Odysseus, and the man who named him. Od. 19.394-466

Dryope.note: A nymph of Arkadia, mother of Pan by Hermes. Hom. Hymn Pan 33-39

Pan.name: Pan (Faunus)
Pan.note: Goat-legged god of the wild, of flocks and of the shepherd's pipe, which he made from the reed Syrinx became. Roman: FAUNUS -- whence fauna. His shout in a lonely place is PANIC, and the word means exactly that: the terror Pan sends. Hom. Hymn Pan

Endymion.note: A shepherd of Latmos so beautiful that Selene asked Zeus to keep him asleep and ageless for ever, and came down to him nightly. Fifty daughters. Apollod. 1.7.5

Orion.note: The giant hunter, loved by Eos and killed by Artemis -- by a scorpion, or by her own arrow when Apollo tricked her into shooting at a speck far out at sea. Set among the stars, with the scorpion behind him: ORION, which is why the two constellations are never in the sky at once. Apollod. 1.4.3-5

Kallisto.note: A huntress of Artemis' band, loved by Zeus in Artemis' own shape, and turned into a bear -- by Hera, or by Artemis for breaking her vow. Her son nearly killed her hunting, and Zeus set them both in the sky as the GREAT BEAR and the Little. Apollod. 3.8.2

Arkas.note: Son of Kallisto, and the man ARKADIA is named for; he taught his people bread, weaving and the hive. Apollod. 3.9.1

Auge.note: Priestess of Athena at Tegea, who bore Herakles a son and hid him in the temple; the goddess sent a famine until he was found. Apollod. 2.7.4, 3.9.1

Telephos.note: Son of Herakles and Auge, king of Mysia, wounded by Achilles' spear on the Greeks' first wrong landing -- and the wound would heal only to rust from that same spear. Apollod. Epit. 3.17-20

Omphale.note: Queen of Lydia, to whom Herakles was sold as a slave for a year in penance for a murder; she wore his lion-skin and he sat spinning wool at her feet, which is the one story Greek art never tired of. Apollod. 2.6.3

Iole.note: Won by Herakles at the bow and refused him by her father; he sacked the city and took her, and it was jealousy of her that made Deianeira send the poisoned shirt. Apollod. 2.7.7

Deidameia.note: Daughter of Lykomedes of Skyros, where Thetis hid Achilles dressed among the king's daughters to keep him from the war; Neoptolemos was born of it. Apollod. 3.13.8

Briseis.note: Taken in a sacked town and given to Achilles, and then taken from him by Agamemnon -- which is the quarrel the Iliad opens on and the reason for every death in it. Il. 1.318-350, 19.282-300

Hippolyte.note: Queen of the Amazons, whose belt was Herakles' ninth labour; by Theseus, or by her sister Antiope, the mother of Hippolytos. Apollod. 2.5.9, Epit. 1.16

Peirithoos.note: King of the Lapiths and Theseus' inseparable friend; they carried off Helen together as a child, and then went down alive to take Persephone, where Peirithoos is sitting still. Apollod. Epit. 1.21-24 Son of Zeus by Ixion's wife, which is why Ixion is not his father and is on the wheel instead.

Eurydike.note: A dryad, Orpheus' wife, who trod on a snake in the grass fleeing Aristaios and died on her wedding day. Georg. 4.457-459

Kinyras.note: King of Cyprus and priest of Aphrodite, and unknowingly his own daughter's lover. Apollod. 3.14.3-4

Myrrha.note: Cursed with desire for her father and lay with him twelve nights disguised; when he saw her he drew his sword, and the gods turned her into the MYRRH tree. She bore Adonis out of the bark. Ov. Met. 10.298-518

people.Adonis: Born of the myrrh tree, and so beautiful that Aphrodite and Persephone both claimed him; Zeus split his year between them, which makes him a plant that dies and returns. Killed by a boar -- Ares, jealous. From his blood, the anemone. Apollod. 3.14.4, Ov. Met. 10.503-739

Narkissos.note: So beautiful and so cold that a rejected lover, Ameinias, killed himself at his door and prayed he would love someone unattainable. He saw his own face in a pool. NARCISSISM, and the flower he left. Ov. Met. 3.339-510

Echo.note: A nymph punished by Hera with the loss of her own speech, able only to repeat the last of what she hears; she loved Narkissos and could not tell him so, and wasted to a voice. ECHO. Ov. Met. 3.356-401

unions.note: Not a union in any ordinary sense -- one could not speak and the other would not listen -- but the pairing the story is. Ov. Met. 3.356-401
A herdsman loved by Pan, who invented pastoral poetry and died of love. Theokritos 1
